notes.meaning: Paul reminds his readers of a basic rule about laws that everyone understands. A law has power over a person only while that person is alive. Once someone dies, legal claims over them come to an end. In the same way, death completely dissolves a person's legal obligations to the law.

Marriage illustrates how death breaks a legal bond. While her husband lives, a woman is bound to him, and marrying another man makes her an adulteress. But when her husband dies, the marriage law no longer has power over her. She is completely free to remarry without breaking God's law.

Believers died to the law through the physical death of Jesus on the cross. Because Christians share in Christ's death, their old relationship to the law as a way of earning God's favor is over. They are now married to the risen Savior, free to produce a harvest of good works that please God.

Before coming to Christ, people lived controlled by fallen human nature. God's commandments commanded good and forbade evil, but corrupt desires reacted against those rules and wanted the forbidden things even more. That rebellion worked through human actions, producing fruit that led straight to spiritual death.

Christians have died to the system that once held them like prisoners. Believers are no longer tied to the law as a rigid written code that demands perfection. Instead, they now serve God gladly from the heart through the life and power of the Holy Spirit.

Paul strongly denies that God's law is evil just because it stirs up sin. The law acts like a mirror or spotlight, showing what sin really is when people do not realize it. For example, people would not understand that evil desires inside the heart are sinful unless the law said, Do not covet.

The sinful nature inside man took advantage of the commandment to rebel even more. When human nature hears a rule that says not to do something, it often wants to do it all the more fiercely. Without the law exposing and challenging it, sin seemed quiet, inactive, and dead.

Paul recalls a time when he felt spiritually secure and blameless as a self-confident Pharisee before the true meaning of the law struck home. But when the commandment reached his conscience in all its holiness, sin woke up and sprang to life. His false sense of goodness vanished, and he realized he was spiritually ruined and dead under God's judgment.

God gave His commandment with the promise of life for anyone who kept it perfectly. But because corrupt human beings fail to obey it, the holy standard only brings a guilty verdict. What was intended to guide people toward life turned out to deliver a death sentence to the sinner.

Sin acted like a crafty enemy, tricking the sinner just as the serpent tricked Eve in the garden. It made false promises of pleasure or self-righteousness, but used the very commandment to lure him into deeper disobedience. In the end, sin used the holy law to strike the sinner dead under God's sentence.

Paul defends God's law from every charge of wrongdoing. The problem is in human rebellion, not in God's commands. The law is pure, its requirements are completely fair, and its purpose is entirely good.

The good law did not cause death; sin did. Sin hijacked something pure and holy to bring about death, showing just how destructive and venomous it really is. By turning God's good gift into an occasion for ruin, sin showed its true, ugly face as something utterly evil.

God's law is spiritual, requiring complete holiness of heart. In contrast, fallen human nature is weak and prone to sin, feeling like an unwilling captive sold into slavery under a cruel master. The traditional view understands this as the honest confession of a mature believer who measures himself against God's perfect standard and sees how far short he falls.

differ.view: This describes an unconverted person who is awakened under the law and struggling in his own strength, not a believer living under gospel grace.
This describes the normal, lifelong conflict of a true believer who hates sin yet grieves over the remnants of corrupt nature.
This represents a carnal Christian trying to live a holy life by law and human willpower rather than depending on the Holy Spirit.

notes.meaning: The writer describes a frustrating inner clash between good intentions and bad actions. In his renewed desires he longs to do what is right, yet fails to carry it out. At the same time, the sins he hates still show up in his daily walk.

The fact that a person hates the wrong things he does shows that his conscience agrees with God. By feeling grief over failure, the inner heart confirms that God's law is good and right. Even while stumbling, the struggling person honors the goodness of the commandment.

This statement is not an excuse to dodge personal blame for sin. Rather, it separates the believer's true, renewed self from the power of sin that still lingers in his earthly body. In his deepest desires he wants God, even though indwelling sin still acts like an unwelcome tyrant within him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The lingering pull toward evil after baptism is called concupiscence; it arises from sin and inclines toward sin, but is not considered sin in itself unless a person gives deliberate consent.

notes.meaning: Fallen human nature has no natural power to produce true goodness on its own. The believer has a God-given desire to do what is pleasing to the Lord, but lacks the personal strength to carry it out perfectly. Real spiritual progress requires relying on God's grace instead of human willpower.

Paul repeats the deep sorrow of his struggle to show how persistent the battle is. Even when the heart aims for the good, weakness and corrupt habits cause the believer to stumble. Falling short of complete obedience remains a constant grief to a godly heart.

When a believer stumbles into sin against the real longing of his heart, it shows that sin operates like an intruder in his life. His true loyalty belongs to God, yet inward corruption continues to push against his best intentions. This inner conflict drives the Christian to seek help outside himself.

The writer discovers a regular principle or pattern in spiritual life on earth. Whenever he resolves to do what is right, evil desires and temptations immediately press close to him. Corrupt nature stands ready at every step to oppose holy living.

From the very center of his renewed being, the speaker feels sincere joy and delight in God's holy law. This is far more than intellectual agreement or fear of punishment; it is genuine love for God's righteous will. Delighting in the holiness of God's commands shows the clear mark of a renewed heart.

differ.view: An unrenewed person under the law can admire and delight in the beauty of God's commandments with his mind, even while completely enslaved to sin.
True inward delight in the holiness of God's law is a mark that belongs only to someone who has been born again by the Holy Spirit.

notes.meaning: An opposing power works through bodily appetites and corrupt nature, warring against the renewed mind. Like an attacking army, this principle of sin constantly assaults the soul and drags the person into painful captivity. The battle proves that a believer cannot defeat indwelling sin through personal strength alone.

This agonizing cry bursts forth from someone worn out by the relentless fight against sin. The body of death pictures remaining corruption clinging like a heavy, decaying weight to the soul. Feeling completely unable to free himself, the speaker cries out for divine rescue.

Deliverance comes only through God's grace in Jesus Christ our Lord. Paul sums up the ongoing tension: with his renewed mind he loyally serves God's law, but his fallen flesh still pulls toward sin. Complete freedom will come, but victory over sin begins right now in Christ.

differ.view: Deliverance through Jesus Christ breaks the slavery of chapter 7, leading the believer into the victorious freedom described in chapter 8.
The believer lives in a dual state throughout earthly life, being wholly righteous before God in Christ while simultaneously struggling with sin in the flesh.
The final summary shows that even the most mature Christian continues to experience this division between the renewed mind and the flesh until heaven.
